Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette:
Minh was seventy-six and had spent most of his adult life in the United States, but the war had never really ended for him. In 1968, during the Tet Offensive, he had been a young shopkeeper in a small Vietnamese town when North Vietnamese soldiers swept through. They accused him of collaborating, dragged him into a back room, and pinned him face-down on a dirt floor while one of them held a rag soaked in diesel fuel over his mouth and nose. He still remembered the pressure of a knee in his lower back, the slick feel of the rag against his lips, the way the fumes burned his throat. He had been certain he would die. The soldiers eventually let him go, but something in him never got up from that floor.

Now he worked the night shift at a regional warehouse, stacking boxes in a long, dim aisle where the air often carried the faint chemical tang of cleaning solvents and spilled fuel from forklifts. That smell could hit him without any warning-an innocent whiff of diesel near the loading bay would suddenly drop him straight back into the dirt-floor room, his chest locked, his hands trembling. The memory was always the same: hyper-detailed, the grain of the dirt under his cheek, the soldier's boot heel grinding into his calf, the rag pressed so hard that his nose ached for hours afterward. When the memory came, it overwhelmed him. He would have to stop whatever he was doing, set down the box, and press his back against a pallet rack until the feeling passed. His supervisor had noticed and started calling him "the freezer," because he would stand so still for so long.

The warehouse also meant occasional confrontations. Another worker, a younger man, had a habit of crowding into Minh's space during the shift change, barking orders about where pallets should go. Minh had learned to avoid that man entirely, walking the long way around the freezer aisle, because any raised voice made his stomach drop and his mind race back to the back room, to the shouts that had preceded the knee in his spine. Each memory sharpened his vigilance. After an episode, he would spend the rest of his shift scanning the aisles for anyone approaching too quickly, bracing for the next ambush. The cycle had become automatic: a trigger brought the memory, the memory made him hyper-vigilant, hyper-vigilance made him more likely to catch the next trigger.

At home, alone in his small apartment, he could not escape entirely. The smell of frying fish from his neighbor's kitchen-greasy and sharp-sometimes reminded him of the diesel, and he would find himself pressing his own hand over his mouth before he knew what he was doing. He had stopped cooking anything with oil. He had stopped inviting anyone over. The world had shrunk to the path between his apartment and the warehouse, and even that felt mined.

What finally brought Minh to the clinic was a new warehouse manager who had rearranged the storage zones. The cleaning aisle was now next to Minh's station. He could not stop the smell. It came every shift, and the memories came every time, and he was having to lock himself in the break room for twenty minutes just to stop shaking. His supervisor told him if he took one more unscheduled break he would be let go. Minh was afraid of losing his job, but he was more afraid of the moment he walked back into that aisle. He wanted someone to explain why a seventy-six-year-old man could still be held down by a smell.
